Hananiah
hăn-ă-nī'ăh
n. (a common Hebrew name borne both by the false prophet who broke Jeremiah's yoke and by the captive who would not bow at Dura)
From Hebrew Chananyah, “the LORD hath been gracious”, from chanan, to show favour, and Yah. Some fifteen men bear it in Scripture; the Greek form is Ananias.

Biblical Definition

Hananiah is a common and beautiful name — the LORD has been gracious — and Scripture attaches it to two men who define opposite ends of faithfulness. The first is Hananiah of Gibeon, a prophet, who stood in the house of the LORD before the priests and all the people and contradicted Jeremiah with a comforting oracle: within two years Babylon's yoke would be broken and the vessels returned. Then “Hananiah the prophet took the yoke from off the prophet Jeremiah's neck, and brake it” (Jer 28:10), and repeated his promise. Jeremiah went his way, came back with a word, and delivered the sentence: “Hear now, Hananiah; The LORD hath not sent thee; but thou makest this people to trust in a lie” (Jer 28:15). He was told he would die that year, and “so Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month” (Jer 28:17). The second Hananiah is one of the four Judean youths taken to Babylon — “Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah” (Dan 1:6) — renamed Shadrach by the prince of the eunuchs, and known ever after by the name a pagan gave him. He stood before the furnace and said that God was able to deliver, and if not, they still would not serve the golden image. One Hananiah promised deliverance God had not promised; the other refused to demand a deliverance God had not promised.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Hananiah; in sacred history it is a frequent Hebrew name, borne notably by a false prophet of Gibeon and by the companion of Daniel called Shadrach.

expand to see more

HANANIAH, n. A Hebrew name signifying the grace or mercy of Jehovah; in Greek, Ananias.

Hananiah the son of Azur, a prophet of Gibeon, withstood Jeremiah and brake the yoke from his neck.

Being told by Jeremiah that he should die that year, he died in the seventh month.

Hananiah, one of the children of Judah carried to Babylon, was named Shadrach by the prince of the eunuchs.

The name is borne also by a captain of the ward in Nehemiah, and by several Levites and princes.

Key Scripture

Jer 28:10 — "Then Hananiah the prophet took the yoke from off the prophet Jeremiah's neck, and brake it."

Jer 28:15 — "Then said the prophet Jeremiah unto Hananiah the prophet, Hear now, Hananiah; The LORD hath not sent thee; but thou makest this people to trust in a lie."

Jer 28:17 — "So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month."

Dan 1:6 — "Now among these were of the children of Judah, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah:"

Modern Corruption

The mark of the false prophet is taken to be doctrinal strangeness; Hananiah's message was orthodox, patriotic, encouraging, and delivered in the temple — and it was a lie.

expand to see more

Everything about Hananiah looked right. He said “Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel”; he prophesied in the house of the LORD; he promised the restoration of the vessels and the return of the captives; and he performed a prophetic sign, breaking a yoke, exactly as the true prophets did. He was also more encouraging than Jeremiah, which is generally what a congregation is buying. Jeremiah's own reply is startlingly generous — “Amen: the LORD do so” — before he says the thing that decides it: the prophets before us prophesied war and evil, so the prophet who prophesies peace will be known when his word comes to pass. The test Scripture gives is not warmth and not orthodoxy of vocabulary; it is whether the LORD sent him, evidenced by whether the thing happens (Deu 18:22). The modern equivalents are the prosperity announcement, the date-set for the Lord's return, and the “word” delivered over a congregation that no one afterwards audits.

The name itself is the second sermon. Both men were called “the LORD has been gracious.” One traded on the grace of God as a guarantee of comfortable outcomes; the other confessed it while telling a king that God might not deliver him and that he would not bow either way. Grace received rightly makes a man able to stand in front of a furnace; grace presumed upon makes him break other men's yokes and tell them what they wish to hear.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Chananyah (H2608), from chanan (H2603), to be gracious, and Yah (H3050); Greek Hananias (G367).

expand to see more

Hebrew Chananyah (H2608) — Hananiah, “the LORD hath been gracious”.

Hebrew chanan (H2603) — to bend or stoop in kindness, to show favour; the root of chen, grace.

Hebrew motah (H4133) — a yoke-bar; the thing Jeremiah wore and Hananiah broke (Jer 28:10).

Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — a lie, falsehood; what Hananiah made the people trust in.

Aramaic Shadrak (H7715) — Shadrach; the Babylonian name given to Hananiah in Dan 1:7.

Usage

"“Took the yoke… and brake it” — a false sign performed in the temple."

"“Thou makest this people to trust in a lie” — the charge that decided the contest."

"“Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah” — four captives who kept their God and lost their names."
